action_criteria.rationale: Screens metabolic, infectious and thyroid causes of encephalopathy and gives the serum anti-GluN1 result, which supports but cannot replace the CSF assay.

action_criteria.rationale: Excludes HSV encephalitis, structural lesions and overlapping demyelination before LP; it is normal or non-specific in most patients and does not confirm the diagnosis.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1 to 2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges).
Refer urgently to urology for radical inguinal orchiectomy of the right testicular mass, with tumor markers and staging CT, as part of first-line treatment.
Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lacosamide; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.

Admit to the ICU / neurocritical care for a GCS of 12, recurrent seizures and autonomic instability (heart rate to 128 bpm, labile blood pressure, diaphoresis), with airway assessment and cardiac monitoring.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide; given the severity, consider early escalation, and discuss fertility preservation (sperm cryopreservation) before cyclophosphamide.
Treat agitation, insomnia and catatonia with benzodiazepines (lorazepam) first.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioral management; urology for the testicular mass.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

accepted: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis associated with testicular teratoma

differential.key_features: CSF HSV-1 and HSV-2 PCR negative 10 days after onset; MRI medial temporal FLAIR signal without hemorrhage or restricted diffusion; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

differential.diagnosis: Other antibody-mediated encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, anti-Ma2)
differential.key_features: Serum neuronal-surface panel negative (LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA); onconeural antibodies negative, including anti-Ma2, the antibody of testicular germ-cell tumors in young men.
Right temporal electrographic seizures, extreme delta brush, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability, GCS 12 and CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with CSF-specific oligoclonal bands.

differential.diagnosis: Drug-induced psychosis or neuroleptic malignant syndrome
differential.key_features: Urine drug screen and ethanol negative; no antipsychotic exposure; CK only mildly raised (380 U/L).

key_clinical_evidence: Ten-day course after a headache and feverish prodrome: psychosis, disorganized speech with neologisms, staring seizures, orofacial dyskinesias with catatonic posturing, GCS 12 and autonomic instability, all six of the Graus 2016 groups.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titer 1:128) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum positive 1:64 is read with the CSF.

MRI shows subtle bilateral medial temporal FLAIR signal without enhancement or restricted diffusion; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds and excludes HSV encephalitis and structural causes.
EEG shows extreme delta brush and two right temporal electrographic seizures; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.

Testicular ultrasound shows a 1.4 cm solid-cystic right intratesticular mass with calcification and normal markers, with no metastasis on staging CT: orchiectomy is part of first-line treatment and gives the histology.
Earlier immunotherapy and tumor removal are associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Concurrent or subsequent seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia, abnormal EEG, or CSF pleocytosis are red flags that mandate exclusion of anti-NMDAR encephalitis before accepting a psychiatric diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Acute psychiatric presentation (paranoia, hallucinations, bizarre behavior) in a previously well young adult brought in by campus police.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a primary psychiatric diagnosis (first-episode psychosis, brief psychotic disorder) and delays neurologic workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatremia occurs in anti-NMDAR encephalitis but is more typical of anti-LGI1 encephalitis; it needs its own work-up and correction and does not point away from the diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a primary metabolic-encephalopathy framing (SIADH from another cause, dehydration, polydipsia) instead of recognizing SIADH as a known complication of NMDAR-E.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome needs antipsychotic exposure, a markedly raised CK and lead-pipe rigidity; he has had no antipsychotic, and this mild CK rise is explained by seizures, dyskinesias and posturing.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Raises concern for neuroleptic malignant syndrome or rhabdomyolysis when combined with dyskinesias and hyperthermia.

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure 18 cmH2O. Lymphocytic pleocytosis (WBC 45 cells/uL, 92% lymphocytes) with mildly elevated protein (55 mg/dL) and normal glucose (58 mg/dL, CSF/serum ratio 0.61). Four oligoclonal bands present in CSF and absent from matched serum. Gram stain: no organisms; bacterial culture: no growth at 48 hours. HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV and enterovirus PCR not detected. Cytology: reactive lymphocytes, no malignant cells. Anti-NMDA receptor (GluN1) IgG positive on cell-based assay, titer 1:128. Clinical correlation recommended.

contraindications: Class warning: haloperidol and other high-potency dopamine D2 antagonists are associated with severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic malignant-like reactions in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
interactions: No current home medications: no drug-drug interaction with the proposed acute agents.
Acyclovir IV: crystal nephropathy risk; maintain hydration and monitor creatinine, especially with other nephrotoxic drugs.
IVIG: risk of renal impairment and thrombosis; ensure hydration and avoid rapid infusion rates.
High-dose methylprednisolone: hyperglycemia, hypertension and hypokalemia; monitor glucose and electrolytes.
Lorazepam with other sedatives: additive respiratory depression in a patient with reduced consciousness.
Levetiracetam: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interactions; renally cleared.
general.summary: No home medications. Category-level cautions for acyclovir, IVIG, high-dose corticosteroids, benzodiazepines and D2 antagonists listed above.
warnings: Rituximab: screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc) before the first dose.
Cyclophosphamide is gonadotoxic: discuss sperm cryopreservation before treatment.

results.finding: Definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis requires one or more of six major symptom groups and IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies, with CSF testing included; probable disease requires four groups (or three with a teratoma) of rapid onset plus an abnormal EEG or CSF pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands.
results.source: Graus F et al. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404

results.finding: All patients had antibodies in CSF, whereas about 14% were negative in serum; CSF titers related more closely to outcome than serum titers.
results.source: Gresa-Arribas N et al. Lancet Neurol 2014;13:167-177

results.finding: 38% had a tumor, mostly ovarian teratoma; 53% improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy or tumor removal; second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide after first-line failure was associated with better outcome; 81% had mRS 0-2 at 24 months.
results.source: Titulaer MJ et al. Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165

results.finding: Extreme delta brush was found in 7 of 23 adults with anti-NMDAR encephalitis and was associated with a more prolonged illness.
Severe intolerance to antipsychotics (rigidity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, neuroleptic malignant-like reactions) was frequent in patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis exposed to them.
results.source: Lejuste F et al. Neurol Neuroimmunol Neuroinflamm 2016;3:e280

anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosi.summary: Published criteria and cohort data on anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: definite diagnosis rests on CSF IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies; first-line immunotherapy and tumor removal are followed by second-line agents when there is no response.

clinical_pearls: Extreme delta brush was seen in 7 of 23 adults (30%) in Schmitt 2012; it supports but does not establish anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
About a fifth of patients are male; tumors are uncommon in men, and the one to seek is a testicular germ-cell tumor.
Normal serum tumor markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) are expected in a teratoma and do not exclude it.
Psychosis with seizures, a movement disorder and autonomic instability should prompt an autoimmune encephalitis work-up regardless of demographics.
Tumor removal (orchiectomy) is part of first-line treatment and is associated with better recovery and fewer relapses.
metadata.diagnostic_challenge: NMDAR encephalitis in a male patient (atypical demographics) presenting with acute psychosis, initially transported by campus police suggesting substance use. The psychiatric-first presentation, male sex, and police involvement all create cognitive biases away from the correct diagnosis of autoimmune encephalitis with testicular teratoma.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools, 3 red herrings, subtype=P; requires CSF antibody confirmation + MRI/EEG/labs synthesis; severe multistage syndrome demanding ICU-level care and earlier second-line escalation
metadata.revision_reason: Independent Reviewer 2 anti-NMDAR audit: tumor screening tailored by age/sex and moved out of lab payloads; paired serum/CSF anti-GluN1 reachable; routine EEG baseline with selected continuous escalation; blanket CAP CT, FDG-PET and blood cultures removed

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Sean O'Brien is a 19-year-old right-handed Irish-American college freshman (pre-medical student) who was brought to the emergency department by campus police after being found in his dorm room talking to invisible people, smashing objects, and appearing terrified. His roommate, who has known him for 4 months, provides the history as the patient is unable to give a coherent account. The roommate reports that approximately 10 days ago, Sean began acting 'off' — he was more withdrawn than usual, skipped several classes (very uncharacteristic for an academically motivated student), stopped going to basketball practice, and was not eating well. He also complained of a headache and felt 'warm' but did not take his temperature. The roommate initially attributed this to first-semester stress or a mild illness. About 5 days ago, Sean became noticeably paranoid — he accused his roommate of poisoning his water bottle and began locking his belongings in his desk drawer. He started sleeping erratically, sometimes not sleeping at all and pacing the room at night. Three days ago, the roommate witnessed Sean talking to people who were not there, appearing to see things in the corner of the room, and becoming increasingly agitated and combative. He smashed his laptop and threw books across the room. The roommate called campus police this morning when Sean was found standing rigidly in the middle of the room, unresponsive to voice, with his arms held in a fixed position above his head for several minutes before suddenly screaming and attempting to climb out the window. Campus police brought him to the ED in restraints. The roommate emphatically denies any drug use by the patient — they share a small room and the roommate states he would know if Sean used any substances. Sean has no history of psychiatric illness, no prior behavioral episodes, and was functioning at a high level academically until 10 days ago. No family history of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. The roommate notes that Sean's mother has thyroid problems and his older sister has 'some food allergy disease.' There is no history of head trauma.

neurological_exam.additional: During the 45-minute examination, three episodes of intermittent staring spells observed lasting 20-40 seconds each — during these episodes, the patient becomes motionless with fixed gaze, orofacial automatisms (lip smacking), and left arm tonic posturing. Afterwards, he is briefly more confused before returning to his agitated baseline. These episodes are highly suspicious for seizures. Autonomic instability present: blood pressure fluctuating between 110/68 and 158/94, heart rate ranging from 88 to 128, and diaphoresis. Temperature 38.2°C without clear infectious source.
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to assess due to agitation.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal 4 mm, reactive to light bilaterally. Oculocephalic movements intact. Prominent orofacial dyskinesias — repetitive lip smacking, jaw movements, and tongue protrusion occurring every 10-20 seconds. Facial sensation intact to grimace. No facial asymmetry. Hearing appears grossly intact (startles to loud sounds). Gag reflex intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Not assessed — patient unable to stand safely.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 12 (E3V3M6). Agitated and disoriented. Unable to provide coherent history. Speech is disorganized with frequent neologisms and word salad. Intermittently responds to internal stimuli — appears to be experiencing visual hallucinations (talking to invisible people, appearing terrified of something in the corner). Unable to cooperate with formal cognitive testing. Not oriented to person, place, or time.
neurological_exam.motor: Unable to cooperate with formal strength testing. Grossly moves all four extremities spontaneously. Intermittent dystonic posturing of the left arm — sustained wrist flexion and finger extension lasting 5-10 seconds. Bilateral upper extremity catatonic posturing observed when patient is stimulated — arms held in fixed elevated position (waxy flexibility). Tone increased in bilateral upper extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 3+ globally — bilateral biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles hyperreflexia. Bilateral extensor plantar responses (Babinski positive bilaterally).
neurological_exam.sensory: Unable to formally assess due to agitation and inability to cooperate.
